item.title: investingLive Americas market news wrap: Hawkish Fed worries ebb after PPI
item.description:
• US October PPI +6.5% vs +6.6% expected
  • Fed's Goolsbee: We're not on the way to 2% inflation and we have to deal with that
  • Goldman Sachs: We can explain almost the entire US inflation overshoot by tariffs and the war in Iran
  • Fed's Collins: I would think some additional policy tightening is warranted soon
  • Fed's Daly: In all likelihood, we need to raise rates

Markets:

  • USD leads, AUD lags
  • WTI crude oil up 43-cents to $89.17
  • US 10-year yields up 3.8 bps to 5.14%
  • S&P 500 down 0.4%, Nasdaq down 0.9%
  • Gold up $4 to $3880

The PPI numbers were something of a respite to the drumbeat of inflation worries as the main numbers were 0.1 pp below estimates. That was generally balanced by non-stop Fed talk on inflation, with Goolsbee saying the recent CPI number was "borderline alarming" and others striking a similar tone. BofA was out with a note to change its Fed call to three consecutive hikes in Dec, Jan and March. All that helped to keep a bid in the dollar, which finisehd at hte best levels of the day. The euro continues to test the Liberation Day lows.

In equity markets, the closing levels don't tell the story as the selling was heavily concentrated in AI and chip names. AMD led the re-think with an 8% loss and pre-market gains for Nvidia reversed. The thinking is that the US is going to draw a hard line against China sales and remote use, curbing the market and -- ultimately -- allowing China to build its own chip companies. Outside of that, breadth was positive and there were some bright spots like Meta with a 2.8% gain. Next week  features a heavy does of retail earnings so that will be a good check on the consumer.

Iran news was generally quiet but there was talk of a strike on US radar facilities in Bahrain. Iran claims it was hit, the US claims the drones were shot down. There was little or nothing on negotiations, so it appears we've reached a standstill and the oil market wasn't overly volatile.

Have a great weekend.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stock markets slide but the selling is localized around chip names
item.description:
The S&P 500 is down 0.6% today and the Nasdaq down 1.0% but it's not as bad as it looks -- so long as you don't own chip stocks and some AI-related names.

Most stocks in the S&P 500 are higher today with 274 up and 197 down. Similarly, the index is solidly higher on the week. The pain is on the chip side of the equation where there are some harrowing losses in light of the turmoil around Nvidia and next week's Anthropic IPO. The overall resilience is impressive considering the terrible start on Monday, the hot CPI report, Jensen Huang's ouster and the jump in Treasury yields.

The pain today is located in a few well-known names:

  • AMD -8.9%
  • DELL -7.7%
  • CSCO -6.1%
  • WDC -5.2%
  • AVGO -4.9%
  • INTC -3.2%
  • NVDA -2.2%

Those are some big questions about AI but they're not really spreading to the hyperscalers:

  • META +2.8%
  • GOOGL -1.2%
  • AMZN -0.6%

Apple, Visa, Walmart, Costco and JPMorgan are also comfortably higher.

The week ahead is an intense one with the Anthropic IPO but there are also a series of reports that will focus on the health of the consumer and I think that's a critical spot to watch. 

Technically, the S&P 500 bounced off the 200-day last week so that's positive and November-December seasonals are also very strong. If you want contra indicators, The Economist is running this on its cover:

The Fear & Greed index is moderately into 'fear' at 39 while AAII sentiment is at -20.8, including the lowest 'bullish' reading since Sept 16.

I still tend to think the market is vulnerable but I like how Anthropic appears to be setting up the IPO for success. The deal is said to be six-times oversubscribed with time to spare. It would be nice if they don't try to maximize every dollar and allow for a rally in the days afterwards. Even moreso if that can back that up with some bullish news on technology or revenue.

This week, I think CoreWeave helped to put some of the worries to rest and is up on the week despite a 6.7% drop today. That said, it's a dangerous game in the tech trade right now and momentum is paramount.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The US consumer may be hitting a wall. A look at eight indicators
item.description:
The old addage is: Never underestimate the spending power of the US consumer.

That stance has been a remarkably good one for traders. Time after time, Americans have dug into their pockets and kept the economy churning.

But never say never.

San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly was just out with a comment, highlighting that she's "just starting to hear the consumer may be running out of gas."

Now that might not be a big red flag. In the Oct 14 Beige Book, the SF Fed reported: "Retail sales softened slightly. Contacts continued to describeeconomic conditions as bifurcated or K-shaped, with one contact observing that mounting financial pressures on lower-income families have spread to impact middle-income households."

Now the K-shape is nothing new and in that same Beige Book, over half of the districts said spending was driven by high-income households. Still, with the election swinging on affordability, gasoline prices staying high and inflation biting, now would be a time to see cracks.

In the week ahead, we will get earnings from Walmart, Target, Home Depot and others, so that will be the best check. We also get official Octobe retail sales, with economists seeing the closely-watched 'control group' up 0.4% m/m. This could be the week where Wall Street realizes that while it's been breathlessly watching AI and the Anthropic IPO, the foundations of the US economy have been eroding.

For those who don't want to wait a few more days, lets look at the early signs:

  1. Sept retail sales control group was +0.1% vs +0.3% expected
  2. Sept personal income report showed the savings rate at 3.8%, the lowest since Oct 2022
  3. Bank of America cardholder data showed spending per household up 5.8% y/y (nominally), down from 6.2%; lower-income households lead at 5.9%; trading down is at its highest since 2021
  4. Redbook same-store sales up 10.4% y/y in the Oct 31 week
  5. In the McDonald's Q3 report US comps fell 0.2%, the first decline since early 2025; fast-food traffic fell 2.6% industry-wide; the CFO wasn't forecasting a better Q4. Management did report encouraging underlying traffic trends in October
  6. NY Fed expectations for Oct saw the expected chance of missing a debt payment hit 13.8%, the highest since December 2025; 45.3% see higher unemployment in a year, the most since April 2020
  7. Citi luxury card data: luxury card purchases were down 6% y/y in September, following 4% declines in both July and August.
  8. CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor on Nov 11: October retail spending gained 0.2% m/m and 3.6% y/y, with core up 0.3% on the month. That monthly gain was the weakest since November 2025, and CNBC’s own headline called it signs of strain

I don't see any real signs of a cliff here but I will be watching this week's numbers at least as closely as Anthropic's IPO.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Daly: In all likelihood, we need to raise rates
item.description:
• Hard to say policy is restrictive enough
  • In all likelihood, we will need to raise rates
  • A myriad of things are pushing up inflation, which makes it concerning
  • Bias is that rates need to go up

Every single Fed official speaking lately says that rates need to go up, and yet seemingly none of them supported a rate hike two weeks ago. It's baffling.

More:

  • I wouldn't spend a lot of time on the summary of economic projections, it's just a point in time
  • I'm looking at the gap between how consumer sentiment and spending gets closed
  • Watch services ex-housing inflation, it's not moving in the right direction
  • Just starting to hear that the consumer may be running out of gas
This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Earnings week ahead: Nvidia without Jensen, Anthropic’s IPO, and the consumer meets a hiking Fed
item.description:
Earnings season is supposed to be over. Instead, next week might be the most important of the quarter for the macro view.

Nvidia reports days after losing its founder. Anthropic prices what could be the largest equity deal ever. And every major US retailer reports into a rate-hike cycle. October CPI came in hot at 0.4% headline and 0.3% core, a December hike is fully priced with a 12% chance of 50 bps, 10-year yields sit at 5.13% and Brent is above $98.

The AI trade gets two tests in 48 hours: Nvidia’s guide on Tuesday and Anthropic’s pricing on Wednesday. Then the consumer gets its turn.

Here is the macro read, day by day.

Monday

A quiet start, with China doing the talking. XPeng, Baidu, H World and KE Holdings cover Chinese autos, ad spending, hotels and housing in one morning. KE is the one I’d watch. It is the cleanest real-time read on whether property transactions have found a floor.

Tyson Foods is the US name to watch. Protein prices are where households feel inflation after the gas pump. Listen for trade-down from beef to chicken and anything on restaurant demand.

Tuesday

The main event, twice over.

Home Depot reports before the open, with consensus at $3.86 on $42.72 billion in revenue. The numbers matter less than the commentary. Housing turnover was already frozen when the Fed was cutting and now mortgage rates are heading the wrong way. The question for Ted Decker is whether big-ticket projects are getting pushed out again and what pros are saying about backlogs.

Retail sales hit at 8:30 am ET, so you get the company view and the government view within the same hour.

Klarna is an underrated macro report. Buy-now-pay-later delinquencies are an early warning on the low-end consumer. Disney parks and Viking tell you whether the high end is still spending on experiences.

Then Nvidia after the close. The Street is at roughly $109.2 billion against the company’s $108 billion guide, and it’s Colette Kress’s first report as interim CEO. The quarter was in the bag before Jensen left, so the print itself is not the risk, the guide is. Nvidia is the single best indicator of the AI capex cycle, and that cycle has been a meaningful slice of US growth. If there’s any wobble in the outlook, it’s not just a Nvidia problem, moreover, we could find out that the China book is a big part of sales and that could now be gone.

Wednesday

Target, TJX and Lowe’s before the open, and the contrast is the story. TJX is a market darling and can still win when consumers trade down. Target loses when they stop buying things they don’t need. If TJX beats and Target misses again, that is a consumer that’s still spending but increasingly picky, the same pattern as the last two years.

Lowe’s is the cross-check on Home Depot, with more DIY and less pro.

ZIM is worth a look for container rates and what the Middle East is doing to shipping lanes. Tencent gives you China gaming and advertising.

The Fed minutes land at 2 pm ET.

After the close, Helmerich & Payne is the one for the oil market. With crude near $100, are US shale producers finally adding rigs? If not, the supply response isn’t coming, and that matters for the inflation outlook. Palo Alto Networks is a read on the boom in AI security. Copa covers Latin American travel demand and jet fuel costs.

The bigger event that night isn’t an earnings report. Anthropic prices its IPO, with 825 million shares marketed at $70 to $78. The top of the range raises $64.35 billion, and with the private placement the total hits $90.4 billion. That values the company at up to $1.4 trillion fully diluted, down from the $2 trillion floated in September.

The macro read is in where it prices. Top of the range, with Nvidia’s guide intact, says there is still deep demand for AI paper even with the 10-year above 5%. A price at the low end, or a cut, says the opposite. Either way, this is a huge amount of supply for the market to absorb in one night, and some of that money has to come from somewhere. Watch the rest of tech into the pricing.

The fundamentals are not the question. Q3 revenue rose more than 12-fold to $17 billion with a 15% adjusted margin. The question is what investors will pay for that at these rates.

Thursday

Walmart. Consensus is $0.64, the top of the company’s $0.62 to $0.64 guided range, on revenue of about $187 billion. BofA is looking for US comps of 2.8% ex-fuel.

No company on earth has better data on the global household. Three things to listen for: whether higher-income shoppers are still trading in, how gasoline at nearly $4 is hitting the low-end basket, and what they say about pricing power into the holidays. The stock has run 18% since the last call, so the bar is high.

Walmart will have to share the screen. Anthropic opens on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, and up to 20% of the deal is set aside for retail, so the first print will be noisy. The first trade matters less than where it settles by the close. The precedent is mixed: SpaceX listed in June and now trades near its IPO price after an August slide. A weak debut two days after a Nvidia report would be hard for the AI trade to shrug off. A strong one resets the mood into Thanksgiving.

Alibaba, PDD and NetEase round out the China picture. Deflation and price wars are the theme, with Alibaba’s cloud capex as the AI offset. Williams-Sonoma is the high-end home read, and it tends to be better than feared.

After the close, Ross and Gap report on the low-to-middle-income apparel shopper. Intuit is a quiet read on small business health. Keysight tells you about electronics and test-equipment orders, a capex indicator that isn’t AI.

Friday

BJ’s Wholesale closes it out. Membership trends and gas-station traffic are worth noting.

The bottom line

Real consumer spending grew 3.8% in Q3. The consumer has not cracked. But the Fed is hiking, oil is high and long rates are above 5%. This week tells us whether that 3.8% was the peak. It also tells us whether the AI trade can lose its frontman and absorb $90 billion in the same week. Those are the two pillars of this economy, and both get tested by Thursday’s close.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs: We can explain almost the entire US inflation overshoot by tariffs and the war in Iran
item.description:
Goldman Sachs is out with a chart that says the US inflation problem is almost entirely two things: tariffs and the Iran energy shock. Take those out and inflation is basically at target.

The latest hard data is ugly. September PCE was 3.6% y/y on headline and 3.1% on core, with gasoline and other energy goods up 9.2% in the month alone. Goldman sees headline peaking just shy of 3.9% right about now and core topping out near 3.3%.

Strip out the two shocks and the picture changes:

  • Headline PCE ex-temporary drivers: roughly 2.2%
  • Core PCE ex-temporary drivers: roughly 2.4%
  • Energy/Iran is worth about 1.5 pp on headline at the peak
  • Tariffs are worth another 0.3-0.4 pp on headline and were closer to a full point on core earlier this year
  • Tariff effects are largely gone by mid-2027; the energy effect fades through late 2027
  • Headline is back near 2.1% and core near 2.4% by the end of 2027

That’s the case for looking through it. Tariffs are a one-time level shift and oil doesn’t rise 30% every year. Hiking rates doesn’t reopen Hormuz.

Here’s the catch: Goldman’s own economists don’t think the Fed will look through it. After Tuesday’s hot October CPI, the third straight upside surprise, they added a hike to their forecast. They now see 25 bps in December and another 25 bps in March, and they pushed the first cut back to December 2027. A month ago they were arguing the Fed might be one-and-done after September.

The rest of the Street is moving faster. Bank of America is just out with a call for hikes in December, January and March, adding January to its forecast. Deutsche Bank has the same three. The market is pricing 86 bps of tightening over the year ahead, which is more than three hikes and more than any of them.

So Goldman is in an odd spot. It says the overshoot is temporary, and it’s still the dove on the Street with two more hikes.

There are a few holes in the temporary story too. First, look at the red line on the core chart. It bottomed near 2.0% in mid-2026 and has climbed to about 2.4% since. That’s the underlying trend moving the wrong way, even after Goldman takes out everything it can. Second, core services ex-housing hit 3.6% y/y in September, tied for the hottest since 2024. Neither tariffs nor crude explains that directly.

Third, “temporary” is carrying a heavy load. Tariff passthrough is in its second year and the energy wedge doesn’t fully close until late 2027. That’s nearly three years of above-target inflation on the heels of 2021-23. Expectations don’t care what the decomposition says, and neither does a Fed that had two dissenters asking for a hike in October.

Goldman is probably right on the math. But the Fed is hiking anyway, and the only debate left is how many.

Also, keep an eye on rates, the long end of the Treasury curve is starting to fret again, with US 10-year yields up another 6 bps to 5.16% today.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Goolsbee: We're not on the way to 2% inflation and we have to deal with that
item.description:
• Inflation has spread into categories where prices not driven by energy
  • The jobs market looks stable, if not tightening a bit
  • Rates will eventually go well-below today
  • We have had signs of trouble for several months in a row now
  • Lately we’re not making any progress and if anything, it’s going the wrong way
  • Inflation is rising and proving far more persistent than expected when it was just a matter of supply shocks
  • The Fed "definitely has work to do" to maintain its credibility
  • Services inflation and rising health care costs don't feel like they will change quickly
  • Even if the price of oil goes down rapidly, refining capacity is still very problematic
  • My feeling is that right now we're not on the way to 2% and we have to deal with that
  • Demand-overheating inflation shocks are extremely hard to get rid of
  • Until about six months ago I thought AI overheating was staying in its lane; I’ve begun to change that view
  • The tariff and oil price shocks were supposed to have gone away by now

This is the guy who used to be the most reliable dove on the FOMC. He’s now talking about demand overheating and Fed credibility.

He was pushed on 25 bps versus something faster in December and wouldn’t bite, but he didn’t push back on the premise either. He was also asked about Bessent’s warning, which invoked the ECB hiking in 2008 right before the financial crisis. He was polite about it and then went straight back to inflation persistence.

There’s an out here. If tariffs, oil and the AI squeeze all ease, he’s comfortable going slow. But he’s not forecasting that, he’s hoping for it. Goolsbee votes in 2027.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US October PPI +6.5% vs +6.6% expected
item.description:
• Prior was 6.3%
  • PPI final demand m/m +0.3% vs +0.4  expected
  • Prior m/m +1.3%
  • Ex-food and energy y/y +5.0% vs +5.0%  expected
  • Prior ex-food and energy 5.0% y/y
  • Ex-food and energy m/m +0.3% vs +0.3% expected
  • Prior ex-food and energy +0.7% m/m
  • Ex-food, energy and trade y/y +4.9% vs +5.0% prior
  • Ex-food, energy and trade m/m +0.5% vs +0.5% prior

The market is increasingly concerned about rising inflation but this is a slight relief, with some bids in bonds afterwards and modest USD selling. We will hear from the Fed's Goolsbee on CNBC momentarily and he recently called inflation "borderline alarming". Ahead of the data, the market was pricing in 28.5 bps of hikes for December, which is a bit over a 10% chance of a 50 bps move, with 86 bps in hikes priced in over the coming year.

For background, the Producer Price Index from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics measures the average change in prices that domestic producers receive for their goods, services and construction. It’s released monthly at 8:30 am ET, typically a day or two after CPI, and tracks inflation from the seller’s side rather than the consumer’s.

The headline is the final demand index, which covers output sold for personal consumption, business investment, government and export. Services make up about 68% of it, goods about 29% and construction the rest, so it’s far broader than a gauge of factory-gate prices. Markets focus on two core measures: final demand excluding food and energy, and the narrower measure that also excludes trade services. Trade services capture retailer and wholesaler margins, which swing sharply and often run opposite to input costs, as when gas station margins shrink during an oil spike.

The PPI is still watched as a pipeline indicator. The intermediate demand indexes for processed goods, unprocessed goods and services show cost pressures building at earlier stages of production before they reach consumers.

Its biggest market role today is as an input to core PCE, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge. Components such as portfolio management fees, airline passenger services, physician care and hospital services feed directly into PCE, so economists use CPI and PPI together to estimate core PCE weeks before its release. A surprise in those categories can shift Fed pricing even when the PPI headline looks unremarkable.

PPI data are revised for four months after initial publication, and the revisions are often large enough to change the trend.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq's suckers' rally is approaching a key resistance amid hawkish Fed bets, US-Iran tensions
item.description:
The Nasdaq recovered all the losses from last Thursday’s sharp selloff amid a dip-buying wave and reassessment of AI-related risks.

Nevertheless, this recovery looks increasingly like a “suckers’ rally” amid more hawkish Fed bets, higher Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar.

Moreover, Trump stated yesterday that the US doesn’t need a deal with Iran. This is another major negative growth driver that could eventually put more pressure on the stock market.

Today, we get the US PPI report, but the data is unlikely to change much since we’ve already got a major hawkish repricing following Fed governor Waller’s remarks and the hot US CPI data.

Overall, the outlook for the Nasdaq remains neutral to bearish. We would need an end to the Iran war or a more dovish Fed to get a sustainable bull market.

 

NASDAQ TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see the Nasdaq (US100 CFD contract) is approaching a key resistance zone around the 28,800 level where we have also a major downward trendline for confluence. We can expect the sellers to step in around the resistance, with a defined risk above the trendline, to position for a drop back into the major upward trendline. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to increase the bullish bets into new all-time highs.

NASDAQ TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we have a minor upward trendline defining the bullish momentum. If we get a pullback, we can expect the buyers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk below it, to keep pushing into new highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to pile in for a drop into the major upward trendline, targeting a breakout.

NASDAQ TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, there’s not much we can add here as the sellers will look for short opportunities around the resistance zone or on the break of the upward trendline, while the buyers will look for a bounce around the minor upward trendline or a break above the major downward one to position for new highs. The red lines define average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Todayconclude the week with the US PPI data.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive European session wrap: Wall Street eyes a rebound but rising Treasury yields keep traders on edge
item.description:
Headlines:

  • Wall Street steadies despite Nvidia drama but dip buyers are still walking a tight rope
  • US bond market cracks resurface as higher for longer fears return to haunt Wall Street
  • Higher real yields and stronger US dollar weigh on gold as Trump puts Iran deal in jeopardy
  • Japan prime minister Takaichi fires another verbal warning as USD/JPY flirts with the 160 level
  • How have interest rate expectations changed after this week's events?
  • Germany October wholesale price index +0.4% vs +1.9% m/m prior
  • France October inflation accelerates as energy prices surge, keeping ECB rate hike bets alive
  • Spain inflation remains stubborn in October, keeping ECB rate hike expectations firmly alive
  • Eurozone Q3 GDP unchanged in second estimate as uneven growth clouds the outlook
  • Solana remains under pressure amid hawkish Fed bets and renewed US-Iran tensions. What's next?

Markets:

  • USD leads, AUD lags on the day
  • 10-year Treasury yields up 3.6 bps to 5.139%
  • WTI crude oil flat at $88.72
  • Gold up 0.4% to $3,891
  • Bitcoin down 3.0% to $69,286
  • European stocks little changed; S&P 500 futures +0.2%

It was a modestly calm session in European morning trade, although one can sense that there are still some nerves yet to settle down.

While the Nvidia fiasco is causing a ruckus in Wall Street, US futures are reacting with much calm today and are looking for a light bounce at the open later. That follows from the comeback yesterday to trim losses before the closing bell. Nvidia shares are up by around 1.5% in pre-market, as tech shares continue to grapple with the prospect of more dip buying and a renewed selloff in the bond market.

On the latter, long-end Treasury yields continue to push higher with 10-year yields now on approach to 5.14% and 30-year yields bordering on 5.48% today. Higher borrowing costs are particularly hurtful for growth stocks, especially at a rather sensitive time when tech shares are being called into question amid the enormous spending on AI infrastructure and how that can eventually justify the lofty valuations.

As yields hold higher, the dollar also continues to keep steadier with USD/JPY flirting with breaching the 160.00 mark and AUD/USD down 0.3% to 0.6789 on the day.

Over in Europe, the risk mood is more tentative with regional benchmark indices moving a little lower as the stirring gains from earlier in the week look to be running out of steam. Still, it has been a good week for European stocks as investors managed to brush aside much of the fallout in US tech shares for the most part.

In the commodities space, gold is up 0.4% to $3,891 but is now firmly in a tug of war as buyers and sellers are battling around the 100-week moving average at $3,896 to close out the week. Meanwhile, oil prices are also more tentative with WTI crude down flattish at $88.72 currently.

Looking ahead, all eyes will be on the US producer price data coming up next to see if that will once again reignite inflation fears and rile up the bond market before the week closes.

I'll be away for next week, so I wish everyone a pleasant weekend and catch you again in the week after. Have a good one!

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: How have interest rate expectations changed after this week's events?
item.description:
Rate hikes by year-end

  • Fed: 28 bps (88% probability of 25 bps rate hike at the next meeting; 12% of 50 bps hike)

2027: 88 bps

  • BoE: 21 bps (85% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)

2027: 94 bps

  • RBNZ: 20 bps (82% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)

2027: 83 bps

  • ECB: 20 bps (82% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)

2027: 71 bps

  • BoJ: 19 bps (76% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)

2027: 78 bps

  • BoC: 16 bps (64% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)

2027: 75 bps

  • SNB: 5 bps (82% probability of no change at the next meeting)

2027: 63 bps

  • RBA: 1 bps (94% probability of no change at the next meeting)

2027: 18 bps of rate cuts

  • The 2027 pricing indicates the total amount of tigthening expected by the end of 2027, not how much is expected in 2027 alone.

The Fed has seen the most significant hawkish repricing this week, driven by Fed Governor Waller's hawkish remarks and the hotter than expected US inflation data. Waller said he would support a 25 bps rate hike in December even if inflation improved, while warning that a 50 bps increase could be necessary if inflation surprised to the upside.

October CPI subsequently came in above expectations, with headline inflation rising 0.4% m/m vs 0.3% expected and core CPI increasing 0.3% vs 0.2% expected. The increased US-Iran tensions have added to inflation concerns through the energy channel, reinforcing the hawkish pricing.

The BoE saw a hawkish repricing after the better than expected UK GDP data and some hawkish remarks from MPC members. The BoE already raised rates by 25 bps to 4% at the last meeting, with an 8–1 vote. One member even favoured a larger 50 bps increase.

The main driver remains the inflation outlook. UK CPI accelerated to 3.5% in September, and the BoE expects inflation to approach 5% by mid-2027 as higher energy prices feed through the economy. The stronger than expected activity data and persistent domestic inflation pressures have also strengthened the case for further tightening. The prolonged US-Iran conflict just adds another layer of upside risk to inflation expectations.

The RBNZ unexpectedly kept rates unchanged at 2.75% in October, in a 4–3 vote, despite markets fully pricing a rate hike. The decision reflected concerns about economic uncertainty and the need to assess the effects of previous tightening. Nevertheless, the central bank maintained a tightening bias. Inflation remains above its 1–3% target range. Higher fuel prices and broader underlying inflation pressures could require further tightening. The latest increase in geopolitical tensions adds to those risks.

The ECB has also seen a slightly hawkish repricing amid increasingly hawkish communication from policymakers. ECB's Žigman recently described another December rate hike as a strong possibility, while cautioning that policymakers need more data before deciding. The risk of higher energy prices feeding into wages and broader price-setting behaviour remains a major concern.

The BoJ hawkish repricing was driven by the central bank's increasingly confident assessment that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target. Governor Ueda recently signalled that the December meeting would include a discussion about another rate increase, suggesting that the BoJ is becoming more comfortable with further policy normalisation.

Additionally, Japanese inflation is expected to remain above the 2% target, partly reflecting the impact of higher energy prices. However, there are still divisions within the BoJ, with some policymakers warning that further tightening could undermine the economic recovery.

The BoC is also expected to deliver another rate hike at the next meeting, despite the economic data showing no urgency whatsoever. The central bank already delivered its first rate hike since July 2023 in October, taking the policy rate to 2.5%. The decision reflected a deterioration in the inflation outlook, with persistently elevated oil prices and increasing evidence that businesses will eventually pass higher input costs on to consumers.

The BoC also revised its inflation outlook higher, expecting CPI inflation to average around 3% in 2027. Governor Macklem acknowledged that further tightening might be necessary, although policymakers intend to proceed cautiously given the uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook.

The SNB remains the least hawkish central bank given limited signs of acceleration in underlying inflation. Although headline inflation has increased due to higher energy prices, the SNB has previously stressed that medium-term inflationary pressures remain relatively contained. There is also little evidence of second-round effects, meaning higher energy prices have not yet translated into broader and more persistent inflation. The Swiss franc's safe-haven appeal amid geopolitical uncertainty also provides some additional protection against imported inflation.

For the RBA markets are not pricing any more rate hikes, on the contrary, traders started to price in rate cuts in 2027. The RBA already raised rates 5 times this year, taking the Cash Rate from 3.60% to 4.85% in November. At the last meeting, three members voted against the increase as the appetite for further tightening faded amid softer labour market data.

The central bank's latest projections suggest inflation will remain above 3% until late 2027, but restrictive monetary policy is also expected to weigh on economic activity. Traders expect that the cumulative impact of previous tightening will eventually weaken growth enough to allow rate cuts.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Wall Street steadies despite Nvidia drama but dip buyers are still walking a tight rope
item.description:
Just about everyone seems to be kicking and screaming about how Jensen Huang is tearing down the whole AI boom. And if you listen to the social media echo chamber, you might think tech stocks have already crashed into oblivion. Well, here's a little reality check. As of the close yesterday, the Nasdaq is keeping within 10% from its record highs in early October and is still up by 9% this year.

So, let's take a step back and put the funeral arrangements on hold for now, shall we?

US futures are also continuing to keep steadier today with S&P 500 futures up 0.2% and Nasdaq futures up 0.1%. And that comes despite the bombshell surrounding Nvidia and Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO. The chipmaker is even seeing shares trade up by around 3% now in pre-market. Considering the circumstances, I'd say that's a pretty decent showing.

The steadier mood comes after Wall Street also managed to recover considerably from its lows yesterday. So, it's not to say that dip buyers have packed their bags and ran for the hills.

Having said that, I wouldn't want to mistake that resilience for an all-clear signal either. The Nvidia drama is one thing. However, the bigger headache for tech stocks is that investors are still questioning whether the enormous spending on AI infrastructure can deliver the returns needed to justify lofty valuations.

And with Treasury yields surging again this week, the backdrop is getting even more challenging for equities in general.

10-year Treasury yields have now moved back up to 5.12% with 30-year yields climbing to 5.46%. That's not a good look for growth stocks, particularly when their valuations depend heavily on profits expected years down the road. Higher yields make those future earnings less valuable in today's terms, while offering investors a more attractive alternative in bonds.

So, what's the state of play then for dip buyers at this juncture?

I reckon there's still a case for Wall Street to steady itself, especially when the Nasdaq is only around 8% below its October peak. The panic has certainly been louder than the actual damage so far. However, the important thing to be aware of here is that the margin for error is getting awfully thin.

With AI spending doubts up in the air, bond yields seeing a resurgence once again and Nvidia's leadership uncertainty still lingering, it would be fair to assume that the market will be far less forgiving of bad news.

In other words, the dip buying playbook isn't necessarily thrown out the window. It is just that every wrong move is now going to hurt a whole lot more. For me, that speaks more to a nervous and unforgiving Wall Street than the outright crash or armageddon that some are already calling for.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Eurozone Q3 GDP unchanged in second estimate as uneven growth clouds the outlook
item.description:
• Eurozone Q3 GDP second estimate +0.4% vs +0.4% q/q prelim
  • Prior +0.6%
  • Eurozone Q3 GDP second estimate +1.3% vs +1.3% y/y prelim
  • Prior +1.2%

There are no changes to the initial estimates as the euro area economy holds up in Q3. As a reminder, expectations were for a growth of just 0.2% on the quarter on the initial report. So, the second estimate here mainly reaffirms the beat we saw from two weeks back.

But as mentioned with the release then, there is a bit of a catch when it comes to the relative resilience we're seeing here.

Ireland is the standout in terms of growth numbers with a whopping 5.5% quarterly expansion in Q3. However, let's be reminded of the fact that Ireland has a knack for notoriously volatile GDP figures in the past year and that always warrants some caution. The expansion here was primarily driven by strong activity in multinational-dominated industries, specifically information and communication and manufacturing.

For some context, Ireland's headline growth figure is often a distorted gauge of domestic economic health. That is because it is heavily influenced by contract manufacturing and global profits of multinational corporations that largely flow back to foreign shareholders rather than translating directly into local living standards.

Looking to the bigger names, things aren't as great. Germany managed just 0.2% growth, Italy stagnated at 0.0%, and France even contracted by 0.1%. So, that's hardly an endorsement of economic resilience across the biggest economies in the region.

Similar to how we viewed the initial report, the inflation numbers from France and Spain today are doing little to dissuade the ECB from hiking interest rates again next month. For now, the euro area economy is still holding up somewhat but the overall growth picture remains rather uneven. The question remains whether the broader economy can continue to hold up in Q4 and heading into next year, otherwise the ECB will be facing up against a very tough backdrop of weakening growth and higher inflation at the same time.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

No changes to the preliminary estimates as the final report here reaffirms that Spanish inflation remains stubborn with headline prices keeping near 5% in October. The latest drop in energy prices over the past week or so might help eventually but it will take some time to filter through to the economy.

But for now, inflation pressures are at a rather uncomfortable level for Spain indubitably.

Besides that, core annual inflation is reaffirmed at 3.1% in October and that is unchanged from September. Even so, it is still well above what the ECB would be comfortable with as price pressures continue to pull away from the 2% target.

Alongside the French report from earlier, this just continues to reaffirm that the inflation monster is still a major threat that the ECB has to deal with heading into the final stages of this year.

As things stand, markets are pricing in roughly 82% odds of the ECB making another move in December. For policymakers, they might very well have to go with the flow amid fears that flagging economic growth conditions could make their jobs much tougher come next year.

In the grand scheme of things, it's not a good look for the ECB as they have quite a tough balancing act to work with. On the one hand, they have to deal with more persistent price pressures before they get out of control. On the other, they have to avoid sending the broader economy off a cliff. Tough.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: France October inflation accelerates as energy prices surge, keeping ECB rate hike bets alive

  • Prior +3.1%
  • France October final HICP +3.7% vs +3.8% y/y prelim
  • Prior +3.4%

The final report here confirms a further acceleration in French inflation pressures to start the final quarter of the year. That owes much to another jump in energy prices, which climbed by another 1.9% on the month and are up by 24.1% compared to October last year. The annual estimate is once again after after the estimates for August and September of +16.7% and +21.3% respectively.

That being said, core annual inflation also picked up in October in moving to 1.7% - up from 1.5% in September. That comes as services inflation continues to rise further as well, moving up to 2.6% in October - up from 2.4% in September and 1.9% in August. Ouch.

With that, it reaffirms that price pressures in Europe's second-largest economy are continuing to intensify and at a rather awkward time. With French growth conditions struggling and fiscal risks mounting, it is making for a rather untimely backdrop for policymakers to be dealing with stronger inflation.

As such, that will keep ECB policymakers on their toes in navigating the next steps. For now, the report here will just reinforce expectations of another rate hike in December with markets also pricing in roughly 82% odds of that at the moment.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Germany October wholesale price index +0.4% vs +1.9% m/m prior
item.description:
• Germany October wholesale price index +0.4% m/m
  • Prior +1.9%
  • Germany October wholesale price index 8.8% y/y
  • Prior +8.7%

The breakdownWell, German wholesale prices are continuing to push up in October with the annual estimate hitting 8.8% - the highest since February 2023. The price increase in October was still primarily driven by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has led to a rise in energy products in particular.

The price increase in petroleum products compared to the same month last year was 47.6% and compard to the month before, was 0.9% higher.

Besides that, there was also a significant price increase in wholesale trade for grain, raw tobacco, seeds, and animal feed. That was seen up 21.2% compared to October last year and 0.7% higher compared to September the month before.

Overall, this just reaffirms that price pressures in Germany are holding up to start the final quarter of the year. Businesses will be feeling the pinch here and it will be a question of how much and how willing are they to pass on these added costs to households and consumers. It's all a margin game now essentially.

As for the ECB, the risks of any second-round effects will continue to grow the longer that this trend persists. So, there is that to keep in mind as we look towards next year.

What does this data measure?Germany's wholesale price index measures changes in prices charged by wholesalers to retailers and other businesses. It offers an early indication of cost pressures in the supply chain, which can eventually feed through to consumer inflation.

Why does it matter to markets?Germany is the the euro area's largest economy, making wholesale prices a useful gauge of underlying inflation risks. A sustained increase in wholesale costs could complicate the ECB's efforts to contain inflation, particularly if businesses pass higher costs on to consumers.

How does it fit into the current economic landscape?Wholesale inflation has been accelerating, with September's annual increase reaching its strongest pace since early 2023. Higher energy costs and imported goods prices have been adding pressure, making life more expensive for businesses already dealing with uneven demand.

Current relevance to markets?Moderate. The key question is whether energy-driven inflation pressures are becoming more persistent, even as oil prices have retreated from earlier highs. Another elevated reading would reinforce worries surrounding inflation and the ECB outlook, although CPI and wage developments remain more decisive indicators for policymakers.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
